title: Encoding functions return wrong data instead of failing: hash() silently computes SHA256 for any unknown algorithm; hex_decode() drops the last nibble of odd-length input
existing_state: CreateHashAlgorithm's switch ends with `_ => SHA256.Create()` (Services/Scripting/Functions/EncodingFunctions.cs:104-115), so `hash(data, "crc32")` or `hash(data, "sha3-256")` returns a SHA256 digest with no error — and the intended guard `if (hasher == null) return null;` at EncodingFunctions.cs:67 is dead code because the factory can never return null. Separately, HexDecode sizes its buffer with integer division `value.Length / 2` (EncodingFunctions.cs:86-88), so an odd-length hex string like "abc" decodes only "ab" and silently discards the trailing character instead of rejecting clearly-corrupt input (the existing catch at :91-94 would have returned null had the loop been allowed to hit the bad slice).
recommendation: Change the switch default to return null so the existing null-check at line 67 does its job (hash() then returns null for unknown algorithms, consistent with base64_decode's failure behavior). In HexDecode, return null when value.Length is odd before allocating the buffer. Both are one-line fixes in EncodingFunctions.cs.
user_benefit: Scripts that verify file checksums or decode device-emitted hex get definitively wrong answers today instead of a detectable failure; a checksum comparison against the wrong algorithm fails confusingly, and truncated hex decodes pass through as plausible-looking data.
